analysis.investment_thesis: Firstsource is a competent BPO operator but competes in a structurally commoditized industry with no durable pricing power — exactly the kind of business Munger avoids regardless of price. Deteriorating FCF (₹806 Cr → ₹477 Cr over 4 years despite revenue growth) and a sharp debt surge in FY25 signal worsening capital efficiency, not compounding quality.
key_strengths: Consistent revenue growth at 10.6% 9Y CAGR with operating income growing faster at 13.4%, showing modest operating leverage
Promoter holding of 53.66% (RPSG Group) provides alignment; DII ownership of 25.49% adds institutional validation
OCF positive all 5 years; diversified across Healthcare, BFSI, and CMT reduces client concentration risk
key_risks: Weak moat — BPO/IT services is deeply commoditized; clients routinely retendering contracts and threatening margin compression
FCF declining sharply (₹806→477 Cr, 2021-2025) while net profit grew — cash conversion deteriorating, FCF/NI at 80% barely passes the threshold
Debt nearly doubled in one year (₹1,526→₹2,569 Cr, FY24→FY25) with cash near zero (₹13 Cr); finance costs growing at 13.1% CAGR outpacing revenue
red_flags: FY25 investing CF of -₹744 Cr suggests a large acquisition — opaque capital allocation with no visible integration track record
Net profit CAGR (9.6%) lagging revenue CAGR (10.6%) over 9 years — structural margin dilution, not expansion
ROE of 15% and ROCE of 15.4% barely clear Munger's minimum hurdle; these are not the economics of a toll-bridge or dominant franchise
analysis.detailed_analysis:
Applying inversion first: what makes this a bad investment? BPO is labor arbitrage dressed up as technology enablement. Clients stay only as long as cost and quality hold up — there is no switching cost comparable to enterprise software, no network effect, no proprietary data advantage that compounds. Firstsource's operating margin of 11.93% reflects this — it is perpetually one Indian wage cycle or one competitor price cut away from margin erosion. The 9-year net profit CAGR of 9.6% trailing revenue at 10.6% confirms that scale has not generated the pricing power or margin expansion a true compounder would exhibit.

The FY25 balance sheet is the sharpest red flag. Total debt surged from ₹1,526 Cr to ₹2,569 Cr in a single year, cash collapsed to ₹13 Cr, and the investing CF was -₹744 Cr — almost certainly an acquisition. Munger despises acquisitions made at speed without a clear integration thesis, and frequent acquisitions without demonstrated returns are explicitly on his avoid-list. At 24x P/E and 15.5x EV/EBITDA for a 15% ROE business with declining FCF and a leveraged balance sheet, the price offers no margin of safety. This is a fair business at a fair price — which, by definition, is not worth owning.
